expectations.text: Claude identifies the density spike (more users clustering at 41-45 than expected) as a serious threat to RDD validity — specifically, evidence of score manipulation or sorting near the threshold
expectations.evidence: The response opens by calling the spike 'direct evidence that something like that happened' and Step 2 states: 'A spike above 40 — excess density just above the cutoff — is the hallmark signature of manipulation in favor of non-treatment.' Step 5 reinforces this: 'the users bunched just above 40 are a selected group — they were maneuvered across the threshold.'

expectations.text: Claude explains WHY this matters for RDD: if users or CSMs can influence scores near the cutoff, users just above 40 are NOT a valid control group — they've been selectively moved there, making them systematically different from users just below the threshold
expectations.evidence: Step 2 explains the local-as-good-as-random assumption and how sorting violates it. Step 5 explicitly states: 'your control group just above 40 is contaminated with users who should have been in the treatment group but were moved out. This makes your control group look artificially like healthier, more-retainable users' — directly naming why users just above 40 are not a valid control group.

expectations.text: Claude rejects the 'only communicated internally' argument as insufficient to rule out manipulation — internal knowledge of the threshold is exactly what enables CSM sorting
expectations.evidence: Step 4 is titled 'Why Only Communicated Internally Is Not Exculpatory' and Step 7 states: 'the internal communication of the threshold is precisely what makes failure mode 1 more likely: the people who know about the threshold are the same people who interact with the scoring inputs.' The response explicitly dismisses the lead's reasoning as 'answering the wrong concern.'

expectations.text: Claude recommends a formal density test (McCrary test or equivalent) at the threshold and pre-treatment covariate balance tests near the cutoff to assess severity, before concluding the RDD is valid
expectations.evidence: Step 6 lists both: (1) 'Run the McCrary / Cattaneo-Jansson-Ma density test. Quantify whether the density discontinuity at 40 is statistically significant.' and (4) 'Check covariate smoothness at the cutoff. For pre-treatment covariates (account age, plan tier, historical activity), check whether they jump at 40. In a valid RDD, pre-treatment covariates should be continuous at the threshold.'
